q: The Periodic Table was devised in 1869 by the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev.
e: Mendeleev organized the known elements based on their properties.

q: Mendeleev's Periodic Table was based on the chemical and physical properties of the 118 elements that had been discovered at that time.
e: Mendeleev's Periodic Table was based on the 63 elements that had been discovered at that time.

q: In the modern Periodic Table the 118 known elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number.
e: This modern arrangement resolves inconsistencies present in Mendeleev's original table.

q: There are 18 vertical columns and 7 horizontal rows in the Periodic Table.
e: This is the standard structure of the modern Periodic Table.

q: The vertical columns are called periods.
e: The vertical columns are called groups, while the horizontal rows are called periods.

q: The horizontal rows are called periods.
e: There are 7 periods in the modern Periodic Table.

q: Those elements with similar chemical properties are found in the same columns or groups.
e: Elements in the same group share similar valence electron configurations.

q: Group I elements (except hydrogen) are called the alkali metals.
e: These elements are highly reactive metals.

q: Group II elements are called the halogens.
e: Group II elements are called the alkaline earth metals.

q: Group VII elements are called the halogens.
e: Halogens are highly reactive non-metals found in Group VII.

q: Group 0 elements are known as the noble gases or inert gases.
e: These elements are chemically unreactive due to their stable electron configurations.

q: Groups I and II consist of p-block elements.
e: Groups I and II consist of s-block elements.

q: Groups III, IV, V, VI, VII and group 0 consist of p-block elements.
e: The p-block contains metals, metalloids, and non-metals.

q: Transition elements are d-block elements.
e: Transition metals are located in the central block of the Periodic Table.

q: Inner transition elements (lanthanides and actinides series) are the f-block elements.
e: These are also known as rare earth elements.

q: Lithium is used to make batteries that power electronic devices like digital cameras.
e: Lithium's electrochemical properties make it ideal for lightweight, high-capacity batteries.

q: Sodium vapour lamps give off blue light and are often used in street lamps.
e: Sodium vapour lamps give off yellow-orange light and are often used in street lamps.

q: Fluoride is used in toothpaste to help reduce dental decay.
e: Fluoride strengthens tooth enamel and prevents cavities.

q: Chlorine is used in household bleach to kill bacteria, to whiten clothes, and to clean swimming pool.
e: Chlorine is a powerful disinfectant and bleaching agent.

q: Bromine is used as a fire retardant.
e: Bromine compounds are effective in suppressing flames.

q: Iodine is used in photographic reproduction.
e: Iodine compounds are light-sensitive and historically used in photography.

q: The metalloid silicon is used to make silicon chips.
e: Silicon is a semiconductor, making it essential for modern electronics.

q: Helium is used for filling weather or advertisement balloons and airships.
e: Helium is lighter than air and non-flammable, making it safe for this use.

q: Neon is used in making light and advertising signs.
e: Neon emits a bright red-orange glow when an electric current passes through it.

q: Argon is used to fill tungsten bulbs to provide a reactive atmosphere that promotes oxidation of the filament.
e: Argon is used to fill tungsten bulbs to provide an inert (unreactive) atmosphere that prevents oxidation of the filament.
